idiom_name: shared lock or version token on the cluster root, one lock identity per cluster
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: pick the root of the cluster, make its identity the single lock identity (row lock on the root, lock entry keyed by the root id, or a version token stored with the root) and require every write path to pass through it. Optimistic form: bump the root's token in the same commit that changes any member, and treat a mismatch as 'someone else changed the cluster' — retry or merge. Pessimistic form: acquire the root lock at the start of the edit session, hold it for the session with a timeout and a cleanup path, and release it on commit or abort. In both forms members carry no locks of their own; enforcement lives at the repository/unit-of-work boundary, which must funnel or reject direct member writes. Implementation variants: (A) Shared version token — one version table row per aggregate, all members reference it; lock the version row id in the lock table. (B) Root lock — navigate to aggregate root and lock its id; all members must be reachable from the root. (C) Forced version increment — ORM event listener forces a version bump on the root whenever a member is modified (NHibernate: session.Lock(root, LockMode.Force)), ensuring optimistic concurrency catches inter-member conflicts.
code_sketch:
# optimistic: one token for the whole cluster
begin(); root = load_root(cluster_id); edit_members(root); root.version += 1; commit()
#   -> commit fails if another writer changed the cluster
# pessimistic: lock the root, members are covered
begin(); lock_root(cluster_id, ttl); root = load_root(cluster_id); edit_members(root); commit()
#   -> release_root(cluster_id) on commit or abort
# ORM event listener for forced version increment (NHibernate example)
class ForceVersionUpgradeListener(ISaveOrUpdateEventListener):
    def on_save_or_update(self, event):
        if isinstance(event.entity, IContainSagaData) and not event.session.is_dirty_entity(event.entity):
            event.session.lock(event.entity, LockMode.Force)  # bumps version
pitfalls: A lock identity that is not the root of every member leaves part of the graph unprotected; derive the cluster id from the root and use it in the lock table, the row lock and the version token alike.
Pessimistic locks without a timeout and a cleanup path stay behind after crashes and block the cluster for all other users.
Writes that skip the repository boundary (bulk update, raw SQL, admin script) bypass the root token and silently break the guarantee.
Bidirectional aggregate associations required for forced version increment: members need a direct reference to the root; without it the ORM event listener cannot navigate to bump the version.
One root for everything — a global or tenant-wide lock row serializes the whole application under the name of coarse-grained locking.
Lock escalation: databases may automatically promote many row locks to a table lock when a threshold is exceeded, negating the concurrency benefit without the coarse-grained design intent.

Fencing gap in distributed realizations: if the lock holder crashes after the TTL expires but before the resource is updated, a second holder can acquire the lock and both may attempt to write — use monotonically increasing fencing tokens the resource checks.

Wrong move: put append-only activity data (event or audit-log lines) inside a hot cluster; failure: every append takes the cluster lock, unrelated writers serialize on the root and throughput collapses; instead: model the append-only data as its own cluster with its own lock and let the root observe it through domain events.

Wrong move: hold the pessimistic cluster lock across a remote call, a batch run or user think-time; failure: the root lock is held for seconds or minutes, every other writer queues behind it in a lock convoy and pooled connections are pinned; instead: keep the root lock inside one short transaction and use the optimistic root token for long sessions.

Wrong move: use the root's version token to enforce an invariant that spans two clusters; failure: each transaction passes its own token check while the combined state violates the rule anyway; instead: merge the clusters into one lock boundary, or enforce the rule with a database constraint plus a converging re-check.
